subject: biology
overview: This unit covers how living organisms are recognised, named and classified, from bacteria, protists, fungi, lichens, viruses, viroids and prions to plants (algae to gymnosperms) and animals (non-chordate phyla to chordate classes). It is one of the highest-weightage, most fact-dense units in NEET Biology. Questions mostly test examples, distinguishing features, taxonomic ranks and statement-based traps taken directly from NCERT lines.

topics.explanation: Living organisms show growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation and response to stimuli. Not all of these are defining properties. Growth and reproduction are not, because a sterile mule or worker bee does not reproduce, and non-living crystals and mountains also grow by external accumulation. Growth in living beings is from inside. Metabolism (the sum of all chemical reactions) and consciousness (awareness of surroundings) are defining features, and cellular organisation is the defining feature of life. Biodiversity is the number and types of organisms present on Earth, and about 1.7 to 1.8 million species have been described. Because the variety is so large, organisms must be grouped by observable characters into convenient categories. This makes study easier, reveals relationships and allows universally accepted names.
key_points: Defining properties of life: metabolism, consciousness and cellular organisation
Growth and reproduction are not defining properties of life
Growth in living organisms is intrinsic; in non-living objects it is by surface accumulation
Unicellular organisms grow by cell division, so growth and reproduction are synonymous in them
In vitro metabolic reactions are not living but are living reactions
Humans are the only organisms aware of themselves (self-consciousness)
About 1.7 to 1.8 million species are described
Classification groups organisms into convenient categories based on easily observable characters
topics.neet_tip: Expect assertion-type questions asking whether growth or reproduction is a defining feature of life; the answer is no.
topics.topic: What is living; biodiversity; need for classification

topics.explanation: Taxonomy is the science of characterisation, identification, nomenclature and classification of organisms. Characterisation means describing external and internal structure, cell structure, developmental process and ecological information. Identification means placing an organism correctly, nomenclature means giving it a correct scientific name, and classification means arranging it into groups. Early taxonomy used morphology. Modern taxonomy also uses cytology, anatomy, embryology, physiology, biochemistry and molecular data. Systematics comes from the Latin word systema, meaning systematic arrangement, and Linnaeus used the title Systema Naturae. Systematics is broader than taxonomy because it also includes evolutionary relationships between organisms.
key_points: Basic processes of taxonomy: characterisation, identification, nomenclature, classification
Systematics equals taxonomy plus evolutionary relationships
Systematics is derived from the Latin word systema
Linnaeus wrote Systema Naturae
Modern taxonomy uses morphology, anatomy, cytology, embryology, biochemistry and molecular data
Taxonomic studies of plants, animals and microbes underpin agriculture, forestry and industry
topics.neet_tip: Asked as definition-based single-correct questions on the scope of systematics compared with taxonomy.

topics.explanation: A species is a group of individual organisms with fundamental similarities that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring. Examples are indica in Mangifera indica and tuberosum in Solanum tuberosum. Each category in classification is called a rank, and a taxonomic group at that rank is a taxon. In ascending order the obligate ranks are Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum (Division in plants) and Kingdom. A genus is a group of closely related species, a family is a group of related genera, an order is a group of related families, and so on. Moving from species to kingdom, the number of common characters decreases while the number of organisms in the group increases. Higher categories are aggregates of characters and are therefore harder to define.
key_points: Ascending order: Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum or Division, Kingdom
Genus is a group of closely related species, for example Panthera includes leo, pardus and tigris
Family examples: Felidae (cat and leopard), Canidae (dog), Solanaceae
Order examples: Carnivora (Felidae plus Canidae), Polymoniales (Solanaceae plus Convolvulaceae)
Class Mammalia includes the orders Primata and Carnivora
Phylum is used for animals and Division for plants
Common characters decrease from species to kingdom
Mango: Plantae, Angiospermae (Division), Dicotyledonae (Class), Sapindales (Order), Anacardiaceae (Family), Mangifera (Genus), indica (species)
Man: Chordata, Mammalia, Primata, Hominidae, Homo sapiens
Housefly: Arthropoda, Insecta, Diptera, Muscidae, Musca domestica
Wheat: Angiospermae, Monocotyledonae, Poales, Poaceae, Triticum aestivum

formulas.meaning: Ascending order of taxonomic ranks, used for arrangement and match-the-rank questions

topics.neet_tip: NEET repeatedly asks to arrange ranks in ascending order or to match mango, man, housefly and wheat ranks with their category names.
topics.topic: Concept of species and taxonomical hierarchy

topics.explanation: Binomial nomenclature was given by Carolus Linnaeus. Each scientific name has two components: the generic name, followed by the specific epithet. Names are framed according to universal rules. ICBN (International Code for Botanical Nomenclature) governs plant names and ICZN (International Code of Zoological Nomenclature) governs animal names. Scientific names are in Latin or are Latinised and are written in italics. When handwritten, the genus and species names are underlined separately. The generic name begins with a capital letter and the specific epithet with a small letter. The name of the author appears after the specific epithet in abbreviated form, as in Mangifera indica Linn. Proper names avoid the confusion caused by local names.
key_points: Binomial system was given by Linnaeus and is used worldwide
First word is the genus (capital initial); second word is the specific epithet (small initial)
Names are printed in italics; when handwritten, the two words are underlined separately
Names are Latin or Latinised, irrespective of their origin
ICBN for plants and ICZN for animals
Author citation is abbreviated after the epithet, for example Linn. for Linnaeus
topics.neet_tip: Look for statement questions on the rules of writing names, such as capitalisation, separate underlining and author citation.

topics.explanation: Linnaeus proposed a two-kingdom system, Plantae and Animalia. It failed to separate prokaryotes from eukaryotes, unicellular from multicellular, and photosynthetic from non-photosynthetic organisms such as fungi. R.H. Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom classification in 1969: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. His main criteria were cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships. Monera are prokaryotic, while the other four kingdoms are eukaryotic. Protista are unicellular eukaryotes. Fungi are heterotrophic, absorptive and have chitin walls. Plantae are autotrophic with cellulose walls. Animalia are heterotrophic, holozoic and lack cell walls. Viruses, viroids, prions and lichens are not placed in this system.
key_points: Five-kingdom classification was given by R.H. Whittaker in 1969
Criteria: cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction, phylogenetic relationship
Monera is the only prokaryotic kingdom; its cell wall is non-cellulosic (peptidoglycan in eubacteria)
Fungal cell wall contains chitin, while plants have cellulose walls
Animalia lack cell walls and show holozoic nutrition
Kingdom Protista brings together Chlamydomonas, Chlorella, Paramoecium and Amoeba
Viruses, viroids, prions and lichens are not included in the five kingdoms
topics.neet_tip: Comparison-table questions ask about cell wall composition, nuclear membrane or mode of nutrition across the five kingdoms.

topics.explanation: Monera includes bacteria, the most abundant microorganisms. By shape they are coccus (spherical), bacillus (rod), vibrium (comma) and spirillum (spiral). Archaebacteria live in harsh habitats and have a distinct cell wall; they include halophiles, thermoacidophiles and methanogens. Eubacteria have a rigid wall. They include cyanobacteria with heterocysts, chemosynthetic autotrophs and heterotrophs. Mycoplasma lack a cell wall. Protista are unicellular eukaryotes: chrysophytes, dinoflagellates, euglenoids, slime moulds and protozoans. Fungi are heterotrophic, with chitin walls and hyphae forming a mycelium. Sexual reproduction occurs by plasmogamy, then karyogamy, then meiosis. Fungi are classified as Phycomycetes, Ascomycetes, Basidiomycetes and Deuteromycetes.
key_points: Methanogens live in the gut of ruminants and produce methane in biogas
Cyanobacteria such as Nostoc and Anabaena fix nitrogen in heterocysts and may form blooms
Mycoplasma lack a cell wall, are the smallest living cells and can survive without oxygen
Bacteria reproduce mainly by fission
Chrysophytes (diatoms, desmids) have silica walls forming diatomaceous earth; they are chief producers in oceans
Dinoflagellates have two flagella and cellulose plates; Gonyaulax causes red tides
Euglenoids have a protein-rich pellicle instead of a cell wall, for example Euglena
Slime moulds form a plasmodium; their spores have true walls and are extremely resistant
Protozoans: amoeboid (Amoeba, Entamoeba), flagellated (Trypanosoma causes sleeping sickness), ciliated (Paramoecium), sporozoans (Plasmodium causes malaria)
Phycomycetes are aseptate and coenocytic, with zoospores or aplanospores and zygospores, for example Mucor, Rhizopus, Albugo
Ascomycetes are sac fungi with conidia and ascospores in asci, for example Penicillium, Aspergillus, Claviceps, Neurospora, yeast
Basidiomycetes lack asexual spores and sex organs, and form basidiospores, for example Agaricus, Ustilago (smut), Puccinia (rust)
Deuteromycetes (imperfect fungi) have only an asexual phase, for example Alternaria, Colletotrichum, Trichoderma
In Ascomycetes and Basidiomycetes a dikaryotic (n+n) stage intervenes between plasmogamy and karyogamy
topics.neet_tip: Match questions pair bacterial shapes with names, fungal examples with classes, and plasmogamy, karyogamy and meiosis with their events.
topics.topic: Monera, Protista and Fungi: salient features and classification

topics.explanation: Lichens are symbiotic associations, mutually useful, between algae and fungi. The algal component is the phycobiont and the fungal component is the mycobiont. The phycobiont is autotrophic and prepares food for the fungus. The fungus provides shelter and absorbs mineral nutrients and water for the alga. The association is so close that a lichen looks like a single organism. Lichens are very good pollution indicators because they do not grow in polluted areas, especially those with high $SO_2$. Lichens differ from mycorrhiza, which is a fungus and higher plant root association, as in Pinus.
key_points: Lichen equals alga (phycobiont) plus fungus (mycobiont)
The alga makes food and the fungus provides shelter, water and minerals
Lichens are indicators of air pollution because they are absent in $SO_2$-polluted areas
Lichens are pioneers on bare rock in primary succession
Mycorrhiza is a fungus and plant root association, not a lichen
topics.neet_tip: A direct one-liner is common: lichen is a fungus and alga association, with mycorrhiza or chrysophytes used as distractors.

topics.explanation: Viruses are non-cellular, inert outside a host and become living only inside living cells, so they are obligate parasites. Ivanowsky in 1892 found that the agent of tobacco mosaic disease was smaller than bacteria. Beijerinck called the infectious fluid contagium vivum fluidum, and W.M. Stanley showed viruses could be crystallised. A virus is a nucleoprotein with genetic material that is either RNA or DNA, never both, enclosed in a protein coat called the capsid. Capsids are made of capsomeres. Usually plant viruses have single-stranded RNA and bacteriophages have double-stranded DNA. Viroids were discovered by T.O. Diener in 1971 as the cause of potato spindle tuber disease. They are free RNA without a protein coat and of low molecular weight. Prions are abnormally folded proteins that cause mad cow disease (BSE) and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
key_points: TMV was the first virus studied; Ivanowsky identified it in 1892
Beijerinck coined the term contagium vivum fluidum; Stanley crystallised viruses
A virus contains either DNA or RNA, never both
The capsid is a protein coat made of capsomeres arranged in helical or polyhedral form
Viral diseases include mumps, smallpox, herpes, influenza and AIDS in humans, and mosaic formation, leaf rolling, curling, yellowing and vein clearing in plants
Viroids are smaller than viruses, lack a protein coat and cause potato spindle tuber disease
Prions are infectious misfolded proteins and cause BSE (mad cow disease) and CJD
topics.neet_tip: Disease-to-agent questions are frequent, for example mad cow disease to prions and potato spindle tuber to viroid.

topics.explanation: Algae are simple, thalloid, autotrophic and mostly aquatic. Chlorophyceae are green algae with chlorophyll a and b, starch and a cellulose wall. Phaeophyceae are brown algae with chlorophyll a and c and fucoxanthin; they store laminarin or mannitol and have a cellulosic wall, usually covered on the outside by a gelatinous coating of algin. Rhodophyceae are red algae with chlorophyll a and d and r-phycoerythrin; they store floridean starch and have no flagella. Bryophytes are the amphibians of the plant kingdom. Their dominant gametophyte bears antheridia and archegonia, the sporophyte depends on it, and a protonema stage occurs in mosses. Pteridophytes are the first vascular land plants. The sporophyte is dominant and the prothallus is the gametophyte. Gymnosperms have naked ovules. They are heterosporous, and their male and female gametophytes stay within sporangia retained on the sporophyte.
key_points: Green algae examples: Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Ulothrix, Spirogyra, Chara
Brown algae examples: Ectocarpus, Dictyota, Laminaria, Sargassum, Fucus; zoospores are pear-shaped with two lateral flagella
Red algae examples: Polysiphonia, Porphyra, Gracilaria, Gelidium; agar comes from Gelidium and Gracilaria
Algin comes from brown algae and carrageen from red algae; Chlorella is used as a protein-rich food supplement
Liverworts such as Marchantia reproduce asexually by gemmae
Mosses include Funaria, Polytrichum and Sphagnum; Sphagnum provides peat
Pteridophyte classes: Psilopsida (Psilotum), Lycopsida (Selaginella, Lycopodium), Sphenopsida (Equisetum), Pteropsida (Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum)
Heterospory in Selaginella and Salvinia is a precursor to the seed habit
Gymnosperms: Cycas has coralloid roots with cyanobacteria; Pinus has mycorrhiza; Sequoia is one of the tallest tree species
Gymnosperms have microsporophylls and megasporophylls in strobili or cones; the seeds are naked
Haplontic life cycle: Volvox, Spirogyra, some Chlamydomonas
Diplontic life cycle: seed plants and Fucus
Haplo-diplontic life cycle: bryophytes, pteridophytes, Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia, kelps
topics.neet_tip: Expect pigment and stored-food matching for algae, class identification for pteridophytes (such as Sphenopsida for Equisetum) and gymnosperm statement pairs.
topics.topic: Plant kingdom: algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes and gymnosperms

topics.explanation: Animals are classified by several bases. The first is level of organisation: cellular in Porifera, tissue in Cnidaria and Ctenophora, organ in Platyhelminthes and organ system from Aschelminthes onwards. The second is symmetry: asymmetrical, radial or bilateral. The third is germ layers: diploblastic in Porifera, Cnidaria and Ctenophora, triploblastic in the rest. The fourth is coelom: acoelomate in Platyhelminthes, pseudocoelomate in Aschelminthes and true coelom from Annelida onwards. The fifth is metamerism, first seen in Annelida. Radial symmetry means any plane through the central axis divides the body into identical halves. The non-chordate phyla are Porifera, Cnidaria, Ctenophora, Platyhelminthes, Aschelminthes, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata and Hemichordata. Each has hallmark features such as choanocytes, cnidoblasts, comb plates, flame cells, nephridia, Malpighian tubules, radula and the water vascular system.
key_points: Porifera have a water canal system (ostia, spongocoel, osculum) and choanocytes, for example Sycon, Spongilla, Euspongia
Cnidaria have cnidoblasts and polyp and medusa forms; Obelia shows metagenesis; examples are Physalia, Adamsia, Pennatula, Gorgonia, Meandrina
Ctenophora (sea walnuts) have eight external rows of ciliated comb plates and bioluminescence, for example Pleurobrachia, Ctenoplana
Platyhelminthes are dorsoventrally flat with flame cells, for example Taenia, Fasciola; Planaria shows high regeneration
Aschelminthes are pseudocoelomate and dioecious with sexual dimorphism, for example Ascaris, Wuchereria, Ancylostoma
Annelida are metameric with nephridia; examples are Nereis (parapodia, dioecious), Pheretima and Hirudinaria (monoecious)
Arthropoda is the largest phylum (about two-thirds of named species), with a chitinous exoskeleton, jointed appendages, Malpighian tubules, book gills and book lungs
Arthropod examples: Apis, Bombyx, Laccifer (economic), Anopheles, Culex, Aedes (vectors), Locusta (pest), Limulus (living fossil)
Mollusca is the second largest phylum, with a mantle, radula and ctenidia, for example Pila, Pinctada, Sepia, Loligo, Octopus, Aplysia, Dentalium, Chaetopleura
Echinodermata have a water vascular system and no excretory system; adults are radial and larvae bilateral; examples are Asterias, Echinus, Antedon, Cucumaria, Ophiura
Hemichordata have a proboscis, collar and trunk and a stomochord, for example Balanoglossus, Saccoglossus
topics.neet_tip: Statement questions target symmetry (echinoderm larvae are bilateral), coelom type and the correct phylum for a listed animal or excretory structure.
topics.topic: Animal kingdom: non-chordates up to phyla level

topics.explanation: Chordates have four fundamental features: a notochord, a dorsal hollow single nerve cord, paired pharyngeal gill slits and a post-anal tail. Non-chordates differ by having a ventral solid double nerve cord, no notochord and a dorsal heart, if present. Urochordates have a notochord only in the larval tail, while cephalochordates retain it throughout life. In vertebrates the notochord is replaced by a vertebral column, and the heart is ventral and muscular. Cyclostomata are jawless and form the division Agnatha. Gnathostomata include Pisces (Chondrichthyes and Osteichthyes) and Tetrapoda (Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia). Fishes have a two-chambered heart, amphibians and most reptiles three chambers, and crocodiles, birds and mammals four. Birds and mammals are homeothermous.
key_points: Urochordata: Ascidia, Salpa, Doliolum; Cephalochordata: Branchiostoma (Amphioxus)
Cyclostomata (Petromyzon, Myxine) have a circular suctorial mouth, no scales or paired fins and 6 to 15 pairs of gill slits; they migrate to fresh water to spawn and die after spawning
Chondrichthyes have a cartilaginous skeleton, placoid scales, a ventral mouth, no air bladder and male claspers, for example Scoliodon, Pristis, Carcharodon, Trygon, Torpedo (electric organ)
Osteichthyes have an operculum, an air bladder and cycloid or ctenoid scales, for example Exocoetus, Hippocampus, Labeo, Catla, Clarias, Betta, Pterophyllum
Amphibia have moist scaleless skin, a tympanum, a cloaca and a three-chambered heart, for example Bufo, Rana, Hyla, Salamandra, Ichthyophis (limbless)
Reptilia means creeping or crawling; they have dry cornified skin with epidermal scales or scutes and no external ear openings
Reptile examples: Chelone, Testudo, Chameleon, Calotes, Crocodilus, Alligator, Hemidactylus, Naja, Bangarus, Vipera
Aves have feathers, a beak, pneumatic bones, a crop and gizzard, air sacs and a four-chambered heart, for example Corvus, Columba, Psittacula, Struthio, Pavo, Aptenodytes, Neophron
Mammalia have mammary glands, hair, an external ear (pinna) and are mostly viviparous
Mammal examples: Ornithorhynchus (oviparous), Macropus, Pteropus (flies), Balaenoptera, Delphinus, Camelus, Panthera
Electric organ is found in Torpedo; poison sting in Trygon
topics.neet_tip: Common angles are features that are not chordate characters, the number of heart chambers (with the crocodile exception) and class-to-example matching.
topics.topic: Animal kingdom: chordates up to classes level

key_facts: Whittaker proposed five-kingdom classification in 1969.
Linnaeus gave binomial nomenclature and wrote Systema Naturae.
About 1.7 to 1.8 million species are known.
Mango classification: Mangifera (Genus), Anacardiaceae (Family), Sapindales (Order), Dicotyledonae (Class), Angiospermae (Division).
Ivanowsky (1892) studied TMV; Stanley crystallised viruses; Beijerinck coined contagium vivum fluidum.
T.O. Diener discovered viroids in 1971 as the cause of potato spindle tuber disease.
Prions cause BSE (mad cow disease) in cattle and CJD in humans.
Mycoplasma are the smallest living cells and lack a cell wall.
Methanogens in the rumen of cattle produce methane (biogas).
Gonyaulax, a dinoflagellate, causes red tides.
Trypanosoma causes sleeping sickness and Plasmodium causes malaria.
Albugo causes white rust of mustard; Ustilago causes smut; Puccinia causes rust.
Neurospora is used in biochemical and genetic work; Claviceps produces ergot alkaloids.
Agar comes from Gelidium and Gracilaria (red algae); algin comes from brown algae; carrageen comes from red algae.
Sphagnum provides peat used as fuel and as a packing material.
Equisetum belongs to Sphenopsida, Selaginella to Lycopsida and Psilotum to Psilopsida.
Sequoia (redwood) is one of the tallest trees; Cycas has coralloid roots with cyanobacteria.
Arthropoda is the largest animal phylum and Mollusca the second largest.
Obelia shows metagenesis (alternation of polyp and medusa).
Limulus (king crab) is a living fossil.
Ctenophores show bioluminescence and have eight external rows of ciliated comb plates.
Crocodiles are the only reptiles with a four-chambered heart.
Ornithorhynchus (platypus) is an egg-laying mammal.
Ichthyophis is a limbless amphibian.
Pteropus (flying fox) is a flying mammal; Balaenoptera (blue whale) is the largest mammal.
common_traps: Thinking echinoderms are radial throughout life; adults are radial but larvae are bilaterally symmetrical.
Assuming all reptiles have a three-chambered heart; crocodiles have a four-chambered heart.
Confusing lichen with mycorrhiza; a lichen is an alga and fungus association, while mycorrhiza is a fungus and plant root association.
Mixing up viroids and prions; viroids are free RNA without a protein coat, while prions are misfolded proteins with no nucleic acid.
Writing the ascending order wrongly, for example placing Order above Class; the correct order is Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum, Kingdom.
Believing gymnosperm gametophytes are free-living; they remain within sporangia retained on the sporophyte, and the seeds are naked.
Treating growth or reproduction as defining properties of life; the defining properties are metabolism, consciousness and cellular organisation.
Calling Hemichordata a chordate subphylum; it has a stomochord, not a true notochord, and is placed with non-chordates.
quick_revision: Rank order upward: Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum or Division, Kingdom.
Binomial names: Genus capitalised, epithet in small letters, italicised or underlined separately; ICBN for plants and ICZN for animals.
Five kingdoms (Whittaker 1969): Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
Bacterial shapes: cocci (spherical), bacilli (rod), vibrio (comma), spirilla (spiral).
Fungal sexual cycle: plasmogamy, then karyogamy, then meiosis to give haploid spores.
Fungal classes: Phycomycetes (Rhizopus), Ascomycetes (Penicillium, yeast), Basidiomycetes (Agaricus), Deuteromycetes (Alternaria).
Algal pigments: green (chlorophyll a, b), brown (chlorophyll a, c, fucoxanthin), red (chlorophyll a, d, r-phycoerythrin).
Bryophytes have a dominant gametophyte; pteridophytes are the first vascular plants with a dominant sporophyte; gymnosperms have naked seeds.

Hallmarks: choanocytes (Porifera), cnidoblasts (Cnidaria), comb plates (Ctenophora), flame cells (Platyhelminthes), nephridia (Annelida), Malpighian tubules (Arthropoda), radula (Mollusca), water vascular system (Echinodermata).
Chordate features: notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits, post-anal tail.
Heart chambers: fishes 2; amphibians and most reptiles 3; crocodiles, birds and mammals 4.
